```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(text2vec)
library(glmnet)
library(pROC)
library(sentimentr)
library(knitr)

usc_red  <- "#990000"
usc_gold <- "#E69F00"
blue     <- "#0072B2"

# --- the same 5,000 reviews as Tuesday, with their TRUE labels ---
data("movie_review", package = "text2vec")
dt <- as.data.table(movie_review)
dt[, id := .I]
dt[, label := factor(ifelse(sentiment == 1, "pos", "neg"))]

# --- split 80/20, build the TF-IDF matrix (vocabulary from TRAIN only) ---
set.seed(123)
idx   <- sample.int(nrow(dt), floor(0.8 * nrow(dt)))
train <- dt[idx]
test  <- dt[-idx]

it_train   <- itoken(tolower(train$review), tokenizer = word_tokenizer,
                     ids = train$id, progressbar = FALSE)
vocab_full <- create_vocabulary(it_train)
vocab      <- prune_vocabulary(vocab_full, term_count_min = 10)
vectorizer <- vocab_vectorizer(vocab)
dtm_train  <- create_dtm(it_train, vectorizer)
it_test    <- itoken(tolower(test$review), tokenizer = word_tokenizer,
                     ids = test$id, progressbar = FALSE)
dtm_test   <- create_dtm(it_test, vectorizer)
tfidf      <- TfIdf$new(norm = "l2")
X_train    <- tfidf$fit_transform(dtm_train)
X_test     <- tfidf$transform(dtm_test)

n_train <- nrow(X_train); n_test <- nrow(X_test)
p_full  <- nrow(vocab_full); p_pruned <- ncol(X_train)

# --- the overfitting demo: a logit with (almost) no penalty ---
m0    <- glmnet(X_train, train$label, family = "binomial",
                lambda = 1e-5, alpha = 1)
auc_of <- function(truth, p) as.numeric(auc(roc(
  truth, p, levels = c("neg", "pos"), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)))
p0_tr <- as.numeric(predict(m0, X_train, type = "response"))
p0_te <- as.numeric(predict(m0, X_test,  type = "response"))
auc0_tr <- auc_of(train$label, p0_tr); acc0_tr <- mean((p0_tr >= .5) == (train$label == "pos"))
auc0_te <- auc_of(test$label,  p0_te); acc0_te <- mean((p0_te >= .5) == (test$label == "pos"))
nz0     <- sum(coef(m0)[-1] != 0)

# --- the real thing: lasso with lambda chosen by 5-fold CV on AUC ---
set.seed(123)
cvfit <- cv.glmnet(X_train, train$label, family = "binomial",
                   type.measure = "auc", nfolds = 5, alpha = 1)
lam_min <- cvfit$lambda.min; lam_1se <- cvfit$lambda.1se
p_min   <- as.numeric(predict(cvfit, X_test, s = "lambda.min", type = "response"))
auc_min <- auc_of(test$label, p_min)
acc_min <- mean((p_min >= .5) == (test$label == "pos"))
nz_min  <- sum(coef(cvfit, s = "lambda.min")[-1] != 0)
nz_1se  <- sum(coef(cvfit, s = "lambda.1se")[-1] != 0)

cv_dt <- data.table(lambda = cvfit$lambda, auc = cvfit$cvm,
                    lo = cvfit$cvlo, up = cvfit$cvup)

# --- Tuesday's dictionary, scored on the SAME test reviews ---
test_clean <- gsub("<[^>]+>", " ", test$review)
dict_sc    <- sentiment_by(get_sentences(test_clean))$ave_sentiment
dict_auc   <- auc_of(test$label, dict_sc)
dict_acc   <- mean((dict_sc > 0) == (test$label == "pos"))

# --- the words the model trusts most, each way ---
cf <- coef(cvfit, s = "lambda.min")
cf <- data.table(word = rownames(cf)[-1], beta = as.numeric(cf)[-1])[beta != 0]
top_words <- rbind(cf[order(beta)][1:10][, side := "pushes the score down (negative)"],
                   cf[order(-beta)][1:10][, side := "pushes the score up (positive)"])
top_words <- top_words[order(beta)]
top_words[, word := factor(word, levels = word)]

pct <- function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")
r3  <- function(x) format(round(x, 3), nsmall = 3)
fmt_n <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
```

| Step | Status |

::: {.box}
The number to beat: Tuesday's **dictionary** (sentimentr), which needs no

**`r pct(dict_acc)` accuracy**. If training a model does not beat that, why

:::

# Too Many Columns {.divider}

## The matrix is wider than it is tall {.smaller-90}

Build Tuesday's TF-IDF matrix on the training reviews and count:

- **`r fmt_n(n_train)` training reviews** (80% of the 5,000; the other
  `r fmt_n(n_test)` are locked away as the test set)
- The training reviews contain **`r fmt_n(p_full)` distinct words**. First
  cleanup: drop every word seen **fewer than 10 times**; you cannot learn
  what "ferrari" means for sentiment from 3 examples. That leaves
  **`r fmt_n(p_pruned)` word columns**
- A logit estimates **one coefficient per column**: `r fmt_n(p_pruned)`
  coefficients from `r fmt_n(n_train)` examples. Still almost **two knobs
  per example**

::: {.box}
Week 5's logit was built for a handful of columns. Nothing in it says what
to do when the columns outnumber the rows. Something has to give.
:::

## What actually goes wrong: memorizing {.smaller-90}

We ran that logit, with no guardrails, on the `r fmt_n(p_pruned)`-column
matrix. Here is its report card:

| | Training reviews | Test reviews (never seen) |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Accuracy** | **`r pct(acc0_tr)`** | `r pct(acc0_te)` |
| **AUC** | **`r r3(auc0_tr)`** | `r r3(auc0_te)` |

- `r pct(acc0_tr)` accuracy on the training set: the model found enough
  rare-word combinations to label every training review **perfectly**, like
  a student who memorizes past exams instead of learning the material
- On new reviews it drops to `r pct(acc0_te)`. The gap between the two
  columns **is** overfitting, week 9's trap at full scale
- And it used `r fmt_n(nz0)` words to do it: far too many to read or trust

# The Fix: Regularization {.divider}

## The idea, in plain words {.smaller-90}

Make the model **pay a price for every coefficient it uses**. Instead of
minimizing only its mistakes, it now minimizes:

$$\text{Loss} \;=\; \text{how wrong the predictions are} \;+\; \lambda \times \text{how big the coefficients are}$$

- Week 5's logit minimized only the first term; the second term is **the
  new penalty**
- A word now earns a coefficient **only if it improves predictions enough
  to justify its price**. Rare coincidences ("ferrari" appeared in 3
  positive reviews) are no longer worth paying for
- **λ (lambda) sets the price.** λ = 0: no penalty, the memorizing logit
  from the last slide. λ huge: every coefficient gets forced to zero and
  the model predicts the same probability for everyone
- This is called **regularization**, and the R package that does it for the
  logit is **glmnet**

## The formula, symbol by symbol {.smaller-80}

$$\text{Loss} \;=\; \text{DataFit} \;+\; \lambda \left[\, \alpha \,\|\beta\|_1 \;+\; (1-\alpha)\,\|\beta\|_2^2 \,\right]$$

| Symbol | Name | In plain words |
|:---:|-----|----------|
| DataFit | the logit's loss | how wrong the predictions are on the training data (what week 5's `glm` minimized) |
| $\beta$ | the coefficients | one per word: how much that word moves the score |
| $\|\beta\|_1$ | sum of absolute values | the **lasso** penalty: every nonzero coefficient costs |
| $\|\beta\|_2^2$ | sum of squares | the **ridge** penalty: big coefficients cost extra |
| $\lambda$ | penalty strength | the price dial: 0 = free, huge = everything forced to zero |
| $\alpha$ | the mix | 1 = pure lasso, 0 = pure ridge, in between = elastic net |

::: {.box}
Two dials to set, and only two: **α** (which penalty) and **λ** (how
strong).
:::

## Dial 1, α: lasso or ridge? {.smaller-80}

| | Lasso (α = 1) | Ridge (α = 0) | Elastic net (0 < α < 1) |
|---|------|------|------|
| What it does to coefficients | pushes many to **exactly zero** | shrinks all toward zero, none exactly | a mix of both |
| What you get | a **short list** of words that matter | every word keeps a small say | a compromise |
| Pick it when | you believe **few** features carry the signal | you believe **many** features each matter a little | you are not sure (α = 0.5 is a common default) |

- Lasso's exact zeros are the headline: it does **feature selection for
  free**. Out of thousands of words, it hands you the few hundred worth
  keeping, and you can read them
- Today we use **lasso (α = 1)**: we expect a modest set of opinion words
  to carry most of the signal, and we want the readable shortlist

## Dial 2, λ: do not guess, cross-validate {.smaller-90}

- λ = 0 memorizes; λ = huge predicts the base rate for everyone. The right
  value is somewhere in between, and it **differs for every dataset**, so
  nobody picks it by hand
- The tool you already have: **cross-validation** (week 9). Try a grid of
  λ values; for each one, do 5-fold CV on the **training set** and record
  the average AUC; pick the λ that scores best
- In R this is one line: `cv.glmnet(X, y, family = "binomial",
  type.measure = "auc", nfolds = 5, alpha = 1)` tries about 100 values of
  λ and does all the folding for you

::: {.box}
The test set is **not touched** during any of this. It stays in the vault
until the very end, exactly like week 9.
:::

# Live: Training the Model {.divider}

## The setup, step by step {.smaller-80}

Everything below ran live when this deck was built (the class script has
the code):

| Step | What we did | Guardrail |
|---|---------|--------|
| 1. Split | 80% train (`r fmt_n(n_train)`), 20% test (`r fmt_n(n_test)`), seed 123 | test set in the vault |
| 2. Tokenize | lowercase, split into words | same as Tuesday |
| 3. Vocabulary | all words from the **training** reviews only | the test set must not shape the features |
| 4. Prune | drop words seen < 10 times: `r fmt_n(p_full)` → `r fmt_n(p_pruned)` | can't learn from 3 examples |
| 5. TF-IDF | weights **fit on train**, then applied to both | no leakage |
| 6. Model | `cv.glmnet(...)`, lasso, 5-fold CV on AUC | λ chosen by CV, not by us |

::: {.box}
Note how many of the guardrails are **week 9 rules**, not new text rules.
Text changed the features; the discipline is unchanged.
:::

## The CV curve {.smaller-90}

```{r cv-curve}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.2
p_cv <- ggplot(cv_dt, aes(x = lambda, y = auc)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = up), fill = "grey85") +
  geom_line(color = usc_red, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = lam_min, linetype = "dashed", color = blue) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = lam_1se, linetype = "dashed", color = usc_gold) +
  annotate("text", x = lam_min, y = min(cv_dt$lo) + 0.01, label = "lambda.min",
           color = blue, hjust = 1.1, size = 4) +
  annotate("text", x = lam_1se, y = min(cv_dt$lo) + 0.04, label = "lambda.1se",
           color = usc_gold, hjust = -0.1, size = 4) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "Cross-Validated AUC, Across ~100 Values of the Penalty",
       x = "the penalty strength λ (log scale: tiny on the left, heavy on the right)",
       y = "average AUC across the 5 folds") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
p_cv
```

::: {.smaller-80 .muted}
One point per candidate λ: the average AUC over the 5 folds (grey band:
± one standard error). What happens at the two ends, and where would you
set the dial?
:::

## Reading the CV curve {.smaller-90 .nostretch}

```{r cv-curve-2}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.6
p_cv + labs(title = NULL)
```

- **Left edge** (λ near zero): almost no penalty, the model memorizes, and
  the cross-validated AUC suffers. **Right edge** (heavy λ): the model is
  forced to drop everything and AUC collapses toward 0.5, a coin flip
- The top of the curve is the sweet spot. `cv.glmnet` marks two choices:
  **lambda.min** (blue), the λ with the best average AUC, and
  **lambda.1se** (gold), the heaviest penalty still within one standard
  error of the best: a "just as good, but simpler" option
- The sizes here: lambda.min keeps **`r fmt_n(nz_min)` words**;
  lambda.1se keeps only **`r fmt_n(nz_1se)`**. We use lambda.min today

## The scoreboard {.smaller-80}

All four scored on the **same `r fmt_n(n_test)` test reviews** none of them
saw:

| Model | Needs labeled data? | AUC | Accuracy |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Coin flip | no | 0.500 | 50% |
| Tuesday's dictionary (sentimentr) | no | `r r3(dict_auc)` | `r pct(dict_acc)` |
| Logit, no penalty (λ ≈ 0) | yes | `r r3(auc0_te)` | `r pct(acc0_te)` |
| **Lasso at lambda.min** | yes | **`r r3(auc_min)`** | **`r pct(acc_min)`** |

- Training on labels buys about **`r round(100 * (acc_min - dict_acc))`
  points of accuracy** over the dictionary; that is the price of the
  labels, paid back
- The penalty beats no penalty on every metric **and** uses
  `r fmt_n(nz_min)` words instead of `r fmt_n(nz0)`: better *and* smaller

## The words the model trusts {.smaller-90}

```{r coef-chart}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.4
p_coef <- ggplot(top_words, aes(x = beta, y = word, fill = side)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(c(usc_red, blue),
                    c("pushes the score down (negative)",
                      "pushes the score up (positive)")), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "The 10 Biggest Coefficients, Each Way",
       x = "the word's coefficient in the lasso logit", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + theme(legend.position = "top")
p_coef
```

::: {.smaller-80 .muted}
The lasso's largest surviving coefficients. A review's score is, at heart,
the **sum of the coefficients of the words it contains**. What do you
recognize from Tuesday?
:::

## Reading the words {.smaller-90 .nostretch}

```{r coef-chart-2}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.6
p_coef + labs(title = NULL)
```

- These are Tuesday's counting-chart words again (**worst, awful, waste**
  vs. **great, perfect, excellent**), but this time **learned from the
  labels**, each with a weight, jointly, accounting for all other words
- Of the `r fmt_n(p_pruned)` words, the lasso kept `r fmt_n(nz_min)` and
  set the other `r fmt_n(p_pruned - nz_min)` to exactly zero. What
  survives is a shortlist a manager can read and sanity-check
- This is the quiet payoff of lasso + text: the model is **accurate and
  explainable at the same time**, which the random forest never was

## The code: glm vs. glmnet {.smaller-80}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Week 5, the plain logit**

```r
m <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2,
         data = train,
         family = "binomial")
```

- a formula and a data frame
- fine for a handful of columns
- one model back
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
**This week, the regularized logit**

```r
cv <- cv.glmnet(X_train, y_train,
                family = "binomial",
                type.measure = "auc",
                nfolds = 5, alpha = 1)
p <- predict(cv, X_test,
             s = "lambda.min",
             type = "response")
```

- a **matrix** (sparse is fine), not a formula
- built for thousands of columns
- a whole path of models, one per λ, with CV built in
:::
:::

## The recipe, reusable {.smaller-90}

::: {.box}
**Text classification, end to end:**

1. Get **labeled** examples (positive/negative, spam/not, churned/stayed)
2. Split train/test; the test set goes in the vault
3. Clean, tokenize, build the vocabulary **on the training set**, prune rare terms
4. TF-IDF, fit on train, applied to both
5. `cv.glmnet(..., family = "binomial", type.measure = "auc")`
6. Evaluate on the test set; pick the threshold the business needs (week 9)
7. **Read the surviving words**: do they make sense?
:::

::: {.smaller-90}
The same seven steps run spam filters, support-ticket routers, and
fake-review detectors. Only step 1 changes.
:::

# The Game {.divider}

## The sentiment game {.smaller-80}

Teams, laptops out:
[**`w10-sentiment-analysis-game.R`**](code/w10-sentiment-analysis-game.R)
(also in `w10-code.zip`). Run the top of the script once, then call
`run_tfidf_experiment(dt, ...)` with your own settings. One twist: in the
game the labels come from **Tuesday's dictionary** (that is how teams label
text when nobody has labeled it for them).

| Knob | What it changes |
|---|-----------|
| `ngram_max = 2` | add **bigrams**: "not_good" becomes its own feature |
| `remove_rare`, `term_count_min` | drop rare words (we used 10 today) |
| `remove_popular`, `doc_proportion_max` | drop words that are in almost every review |
| `l2_norm` | normalize each review's TF-IDF row |
| `alpha` | 1 = lasso, 0 = ridge, between = elastic net |
| `use_cv = TRUE` / `lambda_no_cv` | CV-chosen λ vs. a λ you set by hand |

::: {.box}
**The rules:** do not touch the seed or the split. Highest **test AUC**
wins; ties go to the smaller model. You have 25 minutes, then every team
reports its best settings and we discuss *why* they won.
:::
